notes.1a: (i) This question needed careful reading as it asked for the structure in a plant cell not the tissue.
notes.1aii: Many candidates gave the structure where chlorophyll is found rather than naming chlorophyll.
notes.1b: (i) A few candidates confused the unit for the side of a square (cm) and the area (cm2).
notes.1bii: This question was looking for the link between the amount of light and surface area as an adaptation.
notes.1c: (i) Candidates needed to look very carefully at the leaf cross-section and at the different tissues. The shape of the cell should help identify the cell. The end point of each line is important, as epidermis and spongy mesophyll are close together. The line for D labels the cuticle, not the epidermis.
notes.1cii: Many correctly named the xylem and phloem.
notes.1d: (i) Candidates should take notice of the description of images and diagrams. If it is a picture of a leaf, then answers about skin or blood are not suitable. Few candidates identified the guard cell.
notes.1dii: Good attempts were made to describe how this cell adapts the leaf for photosynthesis. Some candidates confused which gases were entering or leaving the stomata.
notes.2a: Many candidates selected the correct conclusions.
notes.2b: (i) Although most candidates understood that the seed needed water for germination, many thought the seed would be photosynthesising so gave carbon dioxide as a requirement. Many confused growth with germination.
notes.2bii: Candidates predicted that the seed would still germinate, but did not notice that the higher, optimal temperature would result in faster germination. The first investigation was at 10 °C, so germination at the middle of the range of temperature should be faster.
notes.2c: A well answered question. A few candidates gave ‘photo trophic’ in error, rather than phototropic. Better responses described the plant root growing into the soil or towards gravity or the centre of the �PAGE�17 0610 Biology June 2025 Earth. A common error was to state that plants grow on the ground which was not sufficiently clear for the mark to be awarded.
notes.3a: Candidates need to be careful with their description of an acid. Whereas highly acidic is correct, high pH describes an alkali.
notes.3b: (i) Most candidates calculated the percentage correctly.
notes.3bii: It was important to select the contaminated water section for the calculation. A few candidates used their own calculation from 3(b)(i).
notes.3c: Candidates showed a good understanding of hygiene and prevention of infection.
notes.3d: Most candidates gave correct answers. Body defence means defence by the body, not how we can protect the body.
notes.3e: This proved to be a challenging question as most candidates did not recognise it as a bacterial cell, but as a plant cell.
notes.4a: Most candidates correctly drew four straight lines.
notes.4b: (i) Few candidates knew which food items are high in iron.
notes.4bii: The question asked for the roles of blood clotting. Some candidates described how blood clots or how blood travels around the body.
notes.5a: Most candidates identified the ribs and diaphragm but not the intercostal muscle.
notes.5b: (i) Candidates need to be careful with naming parts, some confused bronchi with bronchioles.
notes.5bii: Candidates need to understand the different parts of the breathing system and how they are connected.
notes.5c: (i) Candidates were asked to identify the direction of carbon dioxide movement. Many candidates selected arrows for oxygen.
notes.5cii: A few candidates described how gases are exchanged, rather than the features of the alveoli that enable efficient gas exchange.
notes.5d: (i) Most knew the word equation for aerobic respiration.
notes.5dii: Many candidates misread the question and gave a type of cell, rather than a structure within a cell.
notes.6a: This question was generally well answered. A common error was to give net rather than random movement of molecules.
notes.6b: (i) Many candidates gave examples of molecules rather than the three elements.
notes.6c: (i) Many candidates did not recognise the corresponding parts of the model cell. �PAGE�18
notes.6cii: This proved to be a challenging question with only a few realising that starch was a large molecule that would be too large to move through the membrane. It was important to look carefully at the diagram to find the location of the water and the mixture.
notes.6d: Most candidates correctly identified the enzyme.
notes.7a: (i) The scientific name for elephant was given above the photograph. Most candidates selected the correct genus. A few gave the species name.
notes.7aii: Most answered correctly, although a few gave features that were not visible.
notes.7b: (i) Nearly all candidates selected the bearded pig from the food web, as they could clearly see the lines from the pig to the stick insect and the jackfruit tree.
notes.7bii: Most candidates correctly identified a tertiary consumer.
notes.7iii: Most candidates correctly identified a producer.
notes.7iv: Most candidates knew that insects are arthropods.
notes.7v: Most candidates were able to construct a food chain using organisms from the food web. Very few gave a chain using other animals.
notes.7vvi: Most answers were descriptions of a food web rather than an ecosystem.
notes.7c: Most candidates were able give a number of correct answers by selecting data from the graph.
notes.7d: Many excellent answers were seen that showed a wide range of reasons why elephants become endangered. �PAGE�19
notes.key_messages:
Candidates should read the whole question and their answer carefully before moving on. They should ask
themselves if they have answered the actual question. The information they have given may be factually
correct but does not directly answer the question.
notes.general_comments:
Many candidates were well prepared for the exam and had obviously referred to past papers and mark
schemes when preparing. This type of preparation enables candidates to express themselves more clearly.
